questions.question: What are the ways to create a thread in Java, and which should you use?
questions.title: Creating Threads in Java
questions.direct_answer: Java has two main ways to create a thread: extend Thread and override run(), or implement Runnable and pass it to a Thread (or an ExecutorService). Implementing Runnable is preferred because it separates the task from the execution and lets you reuse thread pools; extending Thread ties your class to a single execution and blocks subclassing anything else. In practice you rarely create threads directly — you submit Runnables/Callables to an ExecutorService, which manages a pool for you. There's also the modern Virtual Threads (Project Loom) approach for lightweight concurrency.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the two ways and explain why implementing Runnable (and using an ExecutorService) is preferred over extending Thread.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Extending Thread out of habit, or creating threads with new Thread().start() directly instead of using an ExecutorService.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Two ways: extend Thread or implement Runnable; prefer Runnable + ExecutorService (decouples task from execution, enables pools). Don't create threads directly in production.

sections.title: Two Ways, One Preferred
sections.content: Java gives two main ways to create a thread. You can extend the Thread class and override its run() method, then call start(). Or you can implement Runnable (a task), pass it to a Thread, and call start(). Implementing Runnable is preferred because it separates the task from how it runs — you can pass the same Runnable to a thread pool — and it doesn't consume your one superclass slot. Extending Thread ties your class to a single execution and blocks subclassing anything else. In production code you rarely create threads directly; you submit Runnables or Callables to an ExecutorService, which manages a reusable pool, and Java's modern Virtual Threads (Project Loom) offer lightweight concurrency for I/O-heavy tasks.

sections.title: From a Task to a Running Thread
sections.content:
Both ways end at start() scheduling the thread to run run(); Runnable decouples the task.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[implements Runnable] -->|new Thread\(r\).start\(\)| T[Thread runs run\(\)]
  B[extends Thread overrides run\(\)] -->|.start\(\)| T
```

sections.title: Both ways, plus the ExecutorService you should use
Common Mistakes
items: Calling run() instead of start() — run() runs on the current thread, not a new one.
Creating threads with new Thread().start() directly instead of using an ExecutorService pool.
Extending Thread when you need to subclass something else (you've used your one superclass).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Two main ways: extend Thread (override run()) or implement Runnable; prefer Runnable.
Implementing Runnable separates the task from execution and lets you reuse pools.
In production, submit Runnables/Callables to an ExecutorService; don't create threads directly.
Call start(), not run() — run() executes on the current thread, defeating the point.
Modern Java has Virtual Threads (Project Loom) for lightweight, I/O-heavy concurrency.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Java has two main ways to create a thread. You can extend the Thread class and override its run method, then call start. Or you can implement Runnable — a task — and pass it to a Thread and call start. Implementing Runnable is preferred because it separates the task from how it runs, so you can pass the same Runnable to a thread pool, and it doesn't consume your one superclass slot, where extending Thread ties your class to a single execution and blocks subclassing anything else. In production code you rarely create threads directly; you submit Runnables or Callables to an ExecutorService, which manages a reusable pool, and Java's modern Virtual Threads from Project Loom offer lightweight concurrency for I/O-heavy tasks. A classic mistake is calling run instead of start — run executes on the current thread, not a new one, which defeats the point entirely.
